The notebooks below accompany Unit 4. They are ordinary Jupyter
notebooks and need only `numpy` (plus `matplotlib` for the plots); open
them in JupyterLab, VS Code, or any notebook environment.

## Angle estimation with the Bayes' filter

The cleanest illustration of the filter itself. The angle of a spinning
wheel is to be estimated from a camera that reads the hue of coloured
markings on the wheel, but sees only a limited arc of it and, because
brightness varies, sometimes reports the wrong hue -- though usually one
close to the truth. The angle is quantized into $N$ values, so the belief
is just a vector of $N$ probabilities, and the prediction and correction
steps of the Bayes' filter can be watched updating it directly. This is
the discrete counterpart of the Kalman filter example that opens Unit 6,
and of the Viterbi notebook in Unit 1, which asks for the most likely
*sequence* of angles rather than the belief at each step.

[Download `A_4_angleestimationbayes.ipynb`](A_4_angleestimationbayes.ipynb){download="A_4_angleestimationbayes.ipynb"}

## Position estimation in a grid world

An agent moves through the 77-cell grid world of Unit 3, plus 40 obstacle
cells in which it is invisible, taking a step to an adjacent cell or
staying put with equal probability among the moves the walls permit. When
the agent is visible its position is measured; when it is not, no
measurement arrives at all. The belief over its position must therefore
be propagated through stretches of pure prediction and sharpened again
when the agent reappears -- a good demonstration that a missing
measurement is itself informative, since it rules out every visible cell.

[Download `A_4_K_gridworldBayes.ipynb`](A_4_K_gridworldBayes.ipynb){download="A_4_K_gridworldBayes.ipynb"}

## Remote temperature sensing: when should a sensor transmit?

A battery-powered sensor measures a temperature evolving as
$T_{k+1}=T_k+U_k+w_k$ and transmits to a remote station over a wireless
link, where transmissions are the dominant drain on the battery. The
question is how to keep the remote estimate accurate while transmitting
as little as possible, and the notebook compares two answers: transmit
periodically, or transmit only when the measurement has drifted past a
threshold. The threshold rule is the more interesting one, because
*silence* then carries information -- the station learns that the
temperature is still within the band -- which is exactly the kind of
reasoning the Bayes' filter formalizes.

[Download `A_4_K_RemoteTempSensingBayes.ipynb`](A_4_K_RemoteTempSensingBayes.ipynb){download="A_4_K_RemoteTempSensingBayes.ipynb"}
